content: Analytical chemistry involves the application of standardized experimental methods within the field of chemistry. These methods are applicable across all subdisciplines of chemistry, except for purely theoretical chemistry. Biochemistry focuses on the study of the chemicals, chemical reactions, and chemical interactions that occur within living organisms. It shares a close relationship with organic chemistry, particularly in areas such as medicinal chemistry and neurochemistry. Additionally, biochemistry is closely associated with molecular biology and genetics. Inorganic chemistry is concerned with the study of the properties and reactions of inorganic compounds. The distinction between organic and inorganic chemistry is not absolute, as there is significant overlap, particularly in the subdiscipline of organometallic chemistry. Materials chemistry involves the preparation, characterization, and understanding of substances that possess useful functions. This field represents a relatively new area of study in graduate programs and integrates elements from all classical areas of chemistry, with a focus on fundamental issues unique to materials. Key areas of study include the chemistry of condensed phases (such as solids, liquids, and polymers) and the interfaces between different phases. Nuclear chemistry examines the interactions and assembly of subatomic particles to form atomic nuclei. A significant component of nuclear chemistry is modern transmutation, and the study of nuclides is both a critical outcome and a tool within this field. Organic chemistry is the study of the structure, properties, composition, mechanisms, and reactions of organic compounds. Organic compounds are defined as those based on a carbon skeleton. Physical chemistry investigates the physical and fundamental principles underlying chemical systems and processes. Physical chemists are particularly interested in the energetics and dynamics of these systems and processes. Key areas of study include chemical thermodynamics, chemical kinetics, electrochemistry, statistical mechanics, and spectroscopy. Physical chemistry has substantial overlap with molecular physics and often involves the use of calculus to derive equations. It is closely associated with quantum chemistry and theoretical chemistry but remains distinct from chemical physics. Theoretical chemistry involves the study of chemistry through fundamental theoretical reasoning, often grounded in mathematics or physics. A significant aspect of this field is the application of quantum mechanics to chemistry, known as quantum chemistry. Since the end of World War II, the advent of computers has enabled the systematic development of computational chemistry, which involves creating and applying computer programs to solve chemical problems. Theoretical chemistry overlaps extensively with both theoretical and experimental condensed matter physics, as well as molecular physics. Other specialized fields of chemistry include astrochemistry, atmospheric chemistry, chemical engineering, chemical biology, chemo-informatics, electrochemistry, environmental chemistry, flow chemistry, geochemistry, green chemistry, the history of chemistry, materials science, medicinal chemistry, molecular biology, nanotechnology, organometallic chemistry, petrochemistry, pharmacology, photochemistry, phytochemistry, polymer chemistry, solid-state chemistry, sonochemistry, supramolecular chemistry, surface chemistry, immunochemistry, and thermochemistry. The chemical industry represents a significant economic sector, contributing to 1% of total chemical sales globally.
